name: Femi Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work at a six-person design studio above a bike shop, and most of our clients are small theatres, arts charities and a couple of music venues. I'm in by half nine, I check the print proofs that came back overnight, and then I spend most of the day on posters and season brochures. I still start everything in a sketchbook with a black pen, which my boss Ruth teases me about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a poster clicks, when the type and the picture stop fighting and start talking. What wears me out is the endless rounds of changes from committees, where six people each want the logo bigger. My lunch is usually with Kofi, our junior, at the noodle place on the corner, and we moan about the committees together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a fancy autocomplete and it's not coming for real design. At the studio I'd probably make a joke about how the robots still can't kern a headline. Online I'd share posts from illustrators whose work got scraped, because that part still matters even if AI flops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but I wouldn't be fully relaxed. Ruth already uses an image tool for mood boards, and in this picture she'd keep using it, so some of the early sketching work I love quietly shrinks. My job and pay would be fine, though; theatres want a human who turns up to the dress rehearsal and gets the feel of the show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, sketchbook first, and I'd keep turning down the AI plug-ins Ruth installs. I'd keep putting a fifth of my pay into savings like I do now. I might finally join the designers' union branch Kofi keeps telling me about, because the scraping fight doesn't go away just because the tools stay weak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little itch. It's like a neighbour playing loud music next door: you can live with it, but you notice it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some of the sketching shrinks. What exactly would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first two days of a job, when I fill pages with thumbnails and pick the three that feel right. If Ruth starts handing clients twenty generated mood boards on day one, the client picks a direction before I've even thought. I'd lose the part where I'm actually a designer and keep the part where I'm a typist with taste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would feel it most, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, our junior, because the routine stuff he does is exactly what a tool does a bit faster. Resizing a poster into twelve social media formats is half his week. If that goes to software, Ruth might not hire another junior after him, and that's how young designers lose their first rung.

say: AI is a **fancy autocomplete** and it won't replace real design work.
Artists whose work was **scraped** still deserve credit and payment, even if the tools stay weak.
think: My **job and pay** are safe because theatres want someone at the dress rehearsal.
Ruth's **mood-board tool** could still eat the early sketching days that I enjoy most.
do: Keep **sketching by hand** first and keep declining the AI plug-ins Ruth installs.
Keep saving **a fifth** of each payslip, as I already do.
Join the **designers' union** branch that Kofi has been pushing for months.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small daily **itch** about the tools creeping in.
S0.quote: I'd lose the part where I'm actually a designer and keep the part where I'm a typist with taste.
fieldNote: Femi's worry in the calm picture is about **craft**, not money; his savings and pay feel secure.
He talks about the **junior rung** for Kofi more than about himself.
His refusal of AI tools is a matter of **principle**, tied to artists being scraped.

steps.text: Keep starting every poster in a sketchbook before opening the computer
Join the designers' union branch Kofi keeps mentioning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that design studios need rules: credit for scraped artists, and no firing juniors to save a few hours. At work I'd push Ruth to promise she won't replace Kofi with a subscription. Online I'd probably get into arguments I regret.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in trouble. Writing, checking and planning are a big part of my day: the brief, the copy fitting, the proof checks, the client emails. If software does all that, Ruth needs maybe four of us instead of six, and I'm the one who refuses to touch the tools, so I'd be an easy pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Ruth and ask straight out where she sees me in two years. I'd stop buying new kit and park the holiday money, so my cushion goes from ten months to a year. I'd also look at the screen-printing workshop across town, because printing posters by hand is something software can't do yet, and they run evening classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I picked this job because it felt like the one thing a computer couldn't really do, and in this picture that turns out to be only half true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd never use the tools, but you also say refusing makes you an easy pick. Which way does that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both are true, and I know it sounds stubborn. I'd rather learn a hand skill like screen printing than spend my evenings training a machine on work like mine. If that costs me this job, I'd at least have something that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ada, your partner, the night you heard the studio was cutting back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're fine for a year, because we are, and that I'd rather take a pay cut at a print workshop than become someone who just picks from AI options all day. She teaches, so her job feels steadier than mine right now. That would be a strange flip for us, because I'm the one who earns more.

say: Studios need **clear rules**: credit for scraped artists and no juniors swapped for software.
Ruth should **promise** not to replace Kofi with a subscription.
think: Most of my day is **thinking work**, so a six-person studio could become four.
Refusing the tools makes me an **easy pick** when Ruth decides who stays.
do: Ask Ruth **directly** in the first month where I fit in two years.
Stop buying kit and grow the cushion from ten months to **a year**.
Sign up for **screen-printing** evening classes at the workshop across town.
feel: A **tight chest**, because the job I chose as safe is only half safe.
Some **pride** in choosing a hand skill over training a machine.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn a hand skill like screen printing than spend my evenings training a machine on work like mine.
fieldNote: Femi sees clearly that his **refusal** puts him at risk, and accepts that cost.
His plan points to **hands-on** printing, the part of design that robots reach last.
He notes a **flip** at home: his partner's teaching job now looks steadier than his.

steps.text: Ask Ruth in the first month where his role fits in two years
Stop buying new kit and put the holiday money into savings
Book screen-printing evening classes at the workshop across town
Push Ruth publicly to keep the junior post instead of buying software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a theft on a huge scale: these systems learned from our work and now sell it back cheaper. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd be writing to my local representative about a tax on AI firms. At the studio, I don't think there'd be much left to say, because there might not be much studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my design job is gone within two years, maybe less. Posters and brochures are pure screen work, and if a machine can do almost any thinking work better and cheaper, small theatres with tiny budgets will take it. The only bit with any time left is the physical printing, and that gets about three more years before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd quit waiting and move fast. In the first six months I'd take the screen-printing course full time if I could, and I'd ask the workshop owner for a part-time job pulling prints. I'd keep the savings untouched as long as I could, and I'd stand with the union pushing for public support for people like Kofi who don't have a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor tilting. I'm twenty-seven and I thought I'd just started my career, and it feels like the career is ending before I've done my best work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't much warning. What does the short time change for you, compared with having longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't really study my way into something new; I just have to grab the closest thing with my hands. Printing gives me maybe five years before robots, which is not a career, it's a bridge. With more warning I'd plan; with two years I'd just jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, if your income dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio flat we rent is the big cost, and Ada and I would probably move somewhere cheaper further out. Before that I'd cut the gig tickets and the record shop, which sounds small but it's my whole weekend. I'd keep the savings for rent, not for fun.

say: AI firms **took our work** to train these systems and now sell it back cheaper.
A **tax on AI firms** should fund support for workers who lose their jobs.
think: My **design job** is likely gone within two years because posters are pure screen work.
Printing by hand buys me **about three years** before robots arrive too.
do: Take the **screen-printing course** full time within the first six months.
Ask the workshop owner for **part-time work** pulling prints.
Go to every **union meeting** and write to my local representative.
feel: Like the **floor tilting** just as my career was starting.
**Grief** at losing my best work years before I reach them.
S2.quote: Printing gives me maybe five years before robots, which is not a career, it's a bridge.
fieldNote: Femi expects to **lose his design job** and treats hand printing only as a bridge.
The **short warning** pushes him to jump rather than plan.
His politics come through strongly: **taxing AI firms** and support for colleagues without savings.

steps.text: Enrol full time on the screen-printing course within six months
Ask the print workshop owner for part-time work pulling prints
Lobby his local representative for a tax on AI firms
Move with Ada to a cheaper flat further out of town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but with more time to organise. I'd say designers and illustrators need to get together now, while there's still a few years, and demand a share of what these firms earn. At work I'd try to get the whole studio, Ruth included, to sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes it worse in one way, because I'd watch it coming slowly. Watching the studio lose a theatre client every season would feel like a countdown to the end of my job. My job still goes; it just goes over three or four years instead of overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the screen-printing course on evenings and weekends while I keep my day job. By year two I'd want to be selling my own prints at markets and through a small website, to see if it pays. I'd keep saving, aiming for eighteen months of costs, so I have room when the studio finally folds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. It's less of a shock than the two-year picture, but it's a slow grind of bad news, like watching a tide come in around your ankles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having five years make you more willing to try the AI tools, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I've asked myself that. If I learn them, I'd just be helping them replace me a bit faster. I'd rather put five years into something with my hands that robots reach last, even if that's only a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ada? Does this change any plans you have together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying a place in about three years, and in this picture I'd hold off. I don't want a big loan when I can't see my income past 2031. Ada would probably be annoyed with me, but she'd get it.

say: Designers should **organise now** and demand a share of what AI firms earn.
Everyone at the studio, **Ruth included**, should sign up while there's time.
think: Five years means **watching it come**, one lost theatre client at a time.
My job **still goes**; it just takes three or four years instead of overnight.
do: Take the **screen-printing course** on evenings while keeping the studio job.
Start **selling prints** at markets and online by the second year.
Build savings to **eighteen months** of costs before the studio folds.
feel: **Heavy**, like a tide coming in slowly around my ankles.
S3.quote: Watching the studio lose a theatre client every season would feel like a countdown to the end of my job.
fieldNote: Femi finds the **slower warning** harder emotionally, because the losses arrive one by one.
He again **refuses AI tools**, even with time to learn them.
He would **delay buying a home** with Ada because his income past 2031 is unclear.

steps.text: Take screen-printing classes on evenings while still at the studio
Sell his own prints at markets and online by year two
Build savings to eighteen months of household costs
Hold off on buying a flat with Ada

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse not to. I'd be arguing for retraining money and for laws that make AI firms pay the artists they learned from. At the studio I'd say we should use the decade to make the kind of work only people can make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years gives me a real second act. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives and forty around the time robots do, which is young enough to have built something else. I still think the poster job ends, but I'd have time to land somewhere I chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd keep the studio job and start the screen-printing classes at a relaxed pace. I'd start a small print shop on the side with Kofi, maybe renting a corner of the workshop for a few hundred a month. I'd keep saving as normal and help organise the union branch so the studio's juniors aren't left alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. It's like knowing your lease ends in ten years; you'd rather it didn't, but you can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a second act. What would that look like at forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ideally a little print studio with Kofi, doing gig posters and theatre posters by hand, the kind people frame. Maybe I'd teach printing at a college a couple of days a week. It would pay less, but I'd still be making things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the five-year version felt like a countdown. Why does ten feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I can stop watching the clock and just build. With five I'd be reacting to every lost client. With ten I'd only have to make one good decision a year.

say: Ten years is enough to handle this **fairly**, so there's no excuse.
AI firms should **pay artists** and fund retraining for workers.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** at AGI, young enough to build a second act.
The **poster job** still ends, but I'd land somewhere I chose.
do: Keep the **studio job** and take printing classes at a relaxed pace.
Rent a **corner of the workshop** with Kofi for a small print shop.
Help organise the **union branch** so the juniors aren't left alone.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, like knowing a lease ends in ten years.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I can stop watching the clock and just build.
fieldNote: With a decade, Femi shifts from **reacting** to planning a hand-made print business.
He still expects to **lose the design job**, so his income is at stake.
He plans the future **with Kofi**, showing loyalty to the junior colleague.

steps.text: Keep the studio job while taking printing classes at a gentle pace
Rent a corner of the print workshop with Kofi for a side shop
Help organise the union branch so the studio's juniors get support

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because there's no time to land anywhere. What would help is a proper fund paid by the AI firms that pays people like me to retrain, and real money for juniors like Kofi who have nothing saved. And I'd want a law that says artists get paid when their work trains these systems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss, and it's not the money. I'd miss standing in the back of a theatre and seeing someone pick up the poster I made. A machine making the poster wouldn't take my pay so much as take that moment.

headlineQuote: I'd miss standing in the back of a theatre and seeing someone pick up the poster I made.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old** poster designer at a six-person studio serving small theatres and arts charities.
He sketches **by hand** first and refuses AI tools on principle, tied to artists being scraped.
His **strong savings** keep money worries low in the calm picture, but craft worries remain.
In every AGI picture he expects to **lose his design job** and turns to hand screen printing.
He blames **AI firms** and wants them taxed to fund retraining and support for juniors.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to land anywhere new.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** paid by AI firms, support for juniors, and payment for artists whose work trains AI.
